title: Competition Indices and Environmental Variables Weakly Improve Predictions of Natural Population Fluctuations on Independent Data
content: The debate about the relative importance of interspecific competition and environmental factors in annual population fluctuations has persisted in ecology for many decades. Ecologists face the challenge of determining the extent to which interspecific competition and environmental factors impact population growth rates. We assess the predictive ability of models with and without interspecific competition and environmental covariates to predict population size one year beyond the model-building data. For 11 of 14 datasets a model with interspecific competition and/or environmental factors make better mean ‘absolute’ prediction error. However, none of the models with interspecific competition and/or environmental variables make predictions that are statistically significantly superior to the random walk model. Overall, in about 60% of the sites, models with interspecific competition and environmental variables show performance worse than the random walk baseline model on independent data. We conclude that there is weak evidence that incorporating interspecific competition and/or environmental covariates leads to improved model predictive ability. A thorough assessment of the relative importance of interspecific competition and environmental factors in annual population fluctuations will require evaluating the predictive power of a broader range of models that incorporate ecology of species traits at each generational time.
